Abstract

Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as an effective, interpretable-by-design graph architecture for learning on graphs. They achieve model transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with a simple distance-based reweighting. Despite the effectiveness of GNAN, we identify the following limitations:
i) node-wise relevance scores are computed as a weighted aggregation over all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones;
ii) graph topology is encoded only through shortest-path distances, and structurally distinct graphs may have identical distances;
iii) feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, thus entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects into a single, rescalable term.
To address these limitations, we introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes the contribution of each node into three additive channels: a feature channel, a structural channel, and a feature–structure interaction channel. We center these channels around a training-data baseline that gives every graph equal weight, regardless of its size, making the decomposition well defined and unique.
Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap to standard black-box GNNs. Because every channel is centered and attached to a single node, the explanations of 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} stay local to the node that generates them and reconstruct the model output exactly while providing interpretability at different levels of granularity. 1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning on graphs (Scarselli et al., 2008; Bacciu et al., 2020), with applications in high-stakes scenarios like power grid analysis (Varbella et al., 2024), health forecasting (Hu et al., 2024), software vulnerability detection (Lekeufack Foulefack and Marchetto, 2024), and drug discovery (Wong et al., 2024).
However, the lack of transparency in black-box GNNs has motivated interpretable architectures that trade predictive performance for model transparency (Rudin, 2019).

The prominent examples of these interpretable-by-design architectures are Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2024), which extend Generalized Additive Models (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1986) to graphs.
They learn one univariate function per feature, and linearly combine these over all nodes, scaling the contribution of each node by a learnable, univariate distance function.
This composition of simple, univariate functions gives users full knowledge of how the model aggregated information, and of which features are mostly relevant, enabling model-level understanding and debugging. GNANs have been further extended to temporal, heterogeneous data (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2025), to incorporate parameter-efficient transformations (Siddartha Reddy et al., 2025), and to Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs (Sade et al., 2026).

Despite the effectiveness of GNANs, in this work we identify the following three limitations that can hinder both their downstream performance and their interpretability:
i) the node-wise importance scores extracted by GNAN for node ii do not represent its own contribution, but are a blurred aggregation of the importances of every node; ii) GNAN relies exclusively on shortest-path distances to encode graph structure, potentially missing other informative topological properties.
iii) GNAN multiplies the univariate feature function with the shortest-path distance reweighting, resulting in a less interpretable mixture of feature, distance, and interaction effects.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Attribute-Motif Interaction Graph Additive model (𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}).
𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} relies on motifs automatically discovered from the training set, with each node contributing based on its features and on which motifs it appears in.
The model linearly combines three additive channels – feature, structural, and feature–structure interaction – each centered under a graph-balanced reference distribution that assigns equal mass to each training graph, ensuring the three channels form a unique canonical decomposition.
Summarizing, our main contributions are:

•

We identify three limitations of current graph additive models: node-wise importance scores do not isolate node-local contributions, shortest-path distances miss richer topology, and multiplicative feature–distance coupling obscures the separate feature, distance, and interaction effects.

•

We introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, an interpretable-by-design GNN that replaces distance-based aggregation with automatically mined motifs, enabling the model to capture richer structural patterns while providing disentangled feature- and motif-based contributions.

•

We develop a graph-balanced centering scheme that makes the additive decomposition well-defined and unique, allowing predictions to be decomposed into separate attribute, structural, and attribute–structure interaction contributions.

Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on eight datasets and G-NAMRFF on nine.
Furthermore, in a controlled experiment, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} successfully recovers the known task composition from label supervision alone, and achieves an explanation accuracy of 0.990.99 and 1.001.00 of AUCROC score on two synthetic datasets with known ground-truth explanations.
Although black-box GNNs remain stronger on most real-world benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} narrows the gap while providing an exact, interpretable decomposition of every prediction.

MAEM: Mitigating Recency Bias via a Replay-Free, Capacity-Controlled Dynamic Mixture of Experts for Class-Incremental Graph Learning

Junlin Chen

  
Wenhao Wang

  
Junchao Xu

  
Qingsong Yao

  
Fei Xue

  
Li Sun

  
Xiao Wang

  
Ruijie Wang

Abstract

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads—information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components.
We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved strong performance in learning from graph-structured data (Kipf and Welling 2017; Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec 2017; Veličković et al. 2018). However, real-world graphs often evolve continuously, with new nodes and classes arriving over time (Zhang, Song, and Tao 2022). Class-incremental graph learning requires a model to learn newly emerging classes while retaining its ability to recognize all previously observed ones (van de Ven and Tolias 2019; Zhang, Song, and Tao 2022). In this setting, catastrophic forgetting is primarily manifested as recency bias: because only the newly introduced classes are supervised during the current session, the continually updated model becomes disproportionately biased toward these classes (Hou et al. 2019; Wu et al. 2019b). Consequently, nodes from earlier sessions are increasingly misclassified as belonging to the most recent classes.

Figure 1: Session-wise accuracy matrix of LwF on cora-full. The entry in row ii and column jj denotes the accuracy on session jj after training through session ii.

Figure 1 illustrates this problem using LwF on cora-full (Bojchevski and Günnemann 2018). Although LwF preserves previous predictions through knowledge distillation, its accuracy on earlier sessions rapidly decreases as new classes are learned (Li and Hoiem 2018).
Existing continual learning methods mainly rely on regularization, replay, or architecture expansion (Parisi et al. 2019; De Lange et al. 2022). Regularization-based methods constrain model updates but still repeatedly optimize a shared model on newly arriving classes, which cannot effectively suppress recency bias since such constraints preserve previously learned knowledge only approximately (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017; Aljundi et al. 2018; Liu, Yang, and Wang 2021). Replay-based methods recover historical knowledge by storing previous samples, which introduces additional memory costs and may violate data-retention constraints (Rebuffi et al. 2017; Lopez-Paz and Ranzato 2017; Zhou and Cao 2021). In contrast, architecture-expansion methods allocate separate components to different sessions, naturally reducing interference between old and new knowledge (Rusu et al. 2016; Yoon et al. 2018; Aljundi, Chakravarty, and Tuytelaars 2017).
Nevertheless, existing expansion-based methods face two important limitations. First, many of them are designed for task-incremental learning and require the task identity of each test instance to select the corresponding branch or prediction head (van de Ven and Tolias 2019; Rusu et al. 2016). Progressive Neural Networks (PNNs), for example, assign a separate column to each task and normally rely on task identity during inference (Rusu et al. 2016). This information is unavailable in class-incremental learning, where a test node must be classified among all classes observed so far (van de Ven and Tolias 2019). Second, replacing task identities with a learnable router does not fully solve the problem. Because the router is continually fine-tuned on newly arriving data, it can itself develop recency bias and preferentially assign nodes to recently added experts. Moreover, continuously creating new components leads to unbounded model growth (Rusu et al. 2016; Yoon et al. 2018).
To address these limitations, we propose MAEM, a replay-free and capacity-controlled dynamic Mixture-of-Experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. Abstract

Neural networks operate naturally on finite-dimensional vectors, yet many problems require reasoning about higher-order objects such as distributions, functions, and graphs. Such objects capture relationships within a ground set and rarely admit an explicit compact representation. Moreover, we typically want a compact representation not of a single higher-order object but of an entire family of such objects, including members unseen during training. While a few approaches exist for particular object types, none is designed to work across object types. We propose a unified framework that represents any higher-order object as a fixed-size embedding vector learned over a family of such objects. An encoder maps an object, seen only through a finite set of samples, to an embedding, and a domain-specific decoder supplies the training signal by modeling the object conditioned on that embedding. Since the encoder works only from samples, one architecture serves different object types. Because the decoder is a model already suited to single instances of the object type, the framework inherits that model’s native operations and inductive biases. We instantiate the framework on distributions, functions, and graphs. In each case we show that a single trained model represents an entire family and generalizes to members unseen during training. Furthermore, we demonstrate the downstream utility of these embeddings: interpolating distributions in embedding space, solving differential equations in embedding space, and predicting unseen edges from a graph’s embedding.

1 Introduction

Neural networks have seen a widespread adoption in practically every field of science and engineering where inputs and outputs can be represented as finite-dimensional vectors. In such cases, existing approaches excel at approximating complex relationships between inputs and outputs coming from complex distributions (LeCun et al., 2015; Goodfellow et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2023). However, there is no natural way of capturing distributions, functions, or generally any higher-order objects, as inputs or producing them as outputs. For instance, it is not obvious how to train a neural network to predict the probability density function of an input distribution as there is no general compact representation to provide to the network.

Once we allow higher-order objects as inputs and outputs, it is natural to restrict ourselves to the relevant families of such objects. Examples include families of distributions that share a common parameterization, such as the family of Gaussian distributions parameterized by their mean and covariance, or solutions to differential equations under varying parameters and initial conditions. When a family admits a closed-form parameterization, one can simply feed the parameters into the neural network, but in many cases such a parameterization is not known a priori. Manipulating these higher-order objects, and families thereof, efficiently, with generalization to unseen members, has no general and established solution and is typically handled in ad-hoc and domain-specific manners (Edwards and Storkey, 2016; Kovachki et al., 2023; Narayanan et al., 2017, e.g.,).

These approaches each target a single object type and carry inductive biases that do not transfer to the others. For distributions, kernel mean embeddings (Muandet et al., 2017) depend on a hand-crafted kernel, and the Neural Statistician (Edwards and Storkey, 2016) ties its embeddings to a variational autoencoder. For functions, Neural Processes (Garnelo et al., 2018) learn distributions over functions, and neural operators such as DeepONet (Lu et al., 2021) and FNO (Li et al., 2020) learn maps between function spaces, but impose rigid input assumptions and expose no representation of an individual function. For graphs, most methods embed nodes rather than whole graphs (Hamilton et al., 2017) or learn to generate graphs (Simonovsky and Komodakis, 2018; You et al., 2018; Vignac et al., 2022) without exposing an embedding of any single one. More recently, distribution embeddings have been proposed independently in two distinct domains: as part of a filtering algorithm for state-space models (Solinas et al., 2026b) and as a way to reason across scales in computational biology (Fishman et al., 2025).

(2026b). It couples an encoder, which maps an object given only as a finite set of samples to a fixed-size vector, with a domain-specific decoder that provides the training signal. Because the encoder sees only samples, a single architecture handles very different object types; because the decoder is the model one would normally fit to a single object, the framework lifts its native operations, such as sampling, density evaluation, and spectral reconstruction, from one object to a whole family, while producing a compact representation of each member that is reusable in downstream tasks.

We instantiate the framework on three object types, changing primarily the decoder. For distributions, a generative decoder reconstructs densities from few samples, and the embedding space supports arithmetic and interpolation between distributions. When Missingness Follows the Graph: Beyond Feature Propagation for Missing Features

Enrico Chialà1, Francesco Ferrini2, Antonio Longa3, Bruno Lepri2,

Filippo Maria Bianchi3, Manfred Jaeger4, Veronica Lachi3

1University of Trento 2Fondazione Bruno Kessler

Abstract

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) commonly assume that node features are fully observed, despite missing features being pervasive in real-world applications.
By leveraging the dependence between node features and graph structure, existing graph-specific methods handle missingness by propagating observed feature values along graph edges.
However, these methods have mainly been evaluated in overly optimistic settings, where feature entries are removed independently and uniformly across the graph.
This overlooks realistic scenarios in which missingness propagates among connected nodes, as can occur during localized sensing failures in sensor networks. We formalize this complementary notion as graph-structured mask dependence, where the joint distribution of missingness indicators is shaped by the graph, and introduce a controlled mechanism that instantiates this setting.
We study propagation-based methods theoretically and empirically in this setting, showing that their effectiveness changes substantially compared with the uniformly random regime.
Motivated by this limitation, we propose PEMix, designed to remain effective under challenging graph-structured missingness. Rather than propagating observed values, PEMix uses global structural representations to condition a probabilistic model of incomplete node features before message passing. Experiments under controlled graph-structured missingness and naturally occurring missingness show that PEMix remains robust across complex missingness regimes, with particularly strong performance as missingness becomes severe.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly designed under the assumption that node features are fully observed (Kipf and Welling, 2017; Hamilton et al., 2017; Velickovic et al., 2018).
In practice, this assumption is often violated.
Sensors may fail to record part of their measurements (Braem et al., 2024; Faizin et al., 2019), while communication, acquisition, or infrastructure failures can also lead to missing observations.

Naive approaches rely on simple statistics to fill missing data, treating the feature matrix as tabular (Ferrini et al., 2026; Taguchi et al., 2021).
Graph-specific methods instead leverage the graph topology to handle missingness more effectively.
Most existing methods estimate missing features by propagating the observed values while minimizing a Dirichlet
energy (Rossi et al., 2022).
Methods such as PCFI and FISF extend this principle with confidence-based and iterative propagation schemes (Um et al., 2023; Um et al., 2025) and achieve strong empirical performance on downstream node-level tasks.

However, performance is mostly evaluated on an oversimplified family of missingness patterns.
The standard protocol removes feature entries independently under uniform Missing Completely At Random (MCAR) (Rubin, 1976).
More recent work has considered feature- and label-dependent mechanisms, including Missing Not At Random (MNAR) settings (Ferrini et al., 2026), but these protocols still focus on how missingness depends on feature values or labels.
They leave unexplored a different aspect of the problem: how missingness is conditioned by topology.
The latter is particularly relevant in applications where failures propagate locally.
In sensor networks or smart grids, physical or communication faults often cause entire connected regions of nodes to drop their measured features simultaneously (Marisca et al., 2024).
Consequently, missingness indicators violate standard spatial independence assumptions, generating correlated missing patterns across adjacent nodes.
Thus, the same global missingness rate can lead to very different levels of difficulty for graph-based methods depending on how missing entries are distributed over the graph.
These patterns challenge propagation-based methods: when missing-feature nodes cluster together, there is too little observed information to propagate. We analyze this limitation theoretically and empirically and we propose PEMix, designed to
remain effective under challenging graph-structured missingness.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison of missingness mechanisms.
Left (U-MCAR): Feature entries are dropped independently and uniformly across the graph.
Middle (S-MCAR): Entire feature vectors are missing for randomly sampled nodes, independent of connectivity.
Right (Recursive Transmission, RT): Missingness originates at a shared seed node and expands recursively along graph edges, forming spatially correlated missing regions that challenge propagation-based recovery.

Our contributions are as follows.

1.

We distinguish the classical dependence of the missingness mask on the data from the dependence structure within the mask itself, formalize
graph-structured mask dependence, and introduce Recursive Transmission (RT), a controlled graph-structured mechanism.

2.

We establish a boundary bottleneck for standard feature propagation and show empirically that graph-localized missingness challenges more sophisticated propagation methods.

3.

We propose PEMix to handle clustered missingness where propagation-based approaches fail. It conditions a probabilistic feature model on global structural representations prior to message passing, incorporating graph topology directly without relying on value propagation.

4.

Across controlled graph-structured missingness and real-world datasets, we show that PEMix improves robustness over propagation baselines, achieving particularly strong gains as missingness severity increases.

Abstract

Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) have emerged as an effective, interpretable-by-design graph architecture for learning on graphs. They achieve model transparency by combining per-feature shape functions with a simple distance-based reweighting. Despite the effectiveness of GNAN, we identify the following limitations:
i) node-wise relevance scores are computed as a weighted aggregation over all graph nodes, allowing irrelevant nodes to inherit spurious relevance from relevant ones;
ii) graph topology is encoded only through shortest-path distances, and structurally distinct graphs may have identical distances;
iii) feature and distance information are combined multiplicatively, thus entangling feature, distance, and interaction effects into a single, rescalable term.
To address these limitations, we introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, which represents topology through a vocabulary of mined motifs and decomposes the contribution of each node into three additive channels: a feature channel, a structural channel, and a feature–structure interaction channel. We center these channels around a training-data baseline that gives every graph equal weight, regardless of its size, making the decomposition well defined and unique.
Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on most datasets and narrows the gap to standard black-box GNNs. Because every channel is centered and attached to a single node, the explanations of 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} stay local to the node that generates them and reconstruct the model output exactly while providing interpretability at different levels of granularity. 1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning on graphs (Scarselli et al., 2008; Bacciu et al., 2020), with applications in high-stakes scenarios like power grid analysis (Varbella et al., 2024), health forecasting (Hu et al., 2024), software vulnerability detection (Lekeufack Foulefack and Marchetto, 2024), and drug discovery (Wong et al., 2024).
However, the lack of transparency in black-box GNNs has motivated interpretable architectures that trade predictive performance for model transparency (Rudin, 2019).

The prominent examples of these interpretable-by-design architectures are Graph Neural Additive Networks (GNANs) (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2024), which extend Generalized Additive Models (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1986) to graphs.
They learn one univariate function per feature, and linearly combine these over all nodes, scaling the contribution of each node by a learnable, univariate distance function.
This composition of simple, univariate functions gives users full knowledge of how the model aggregated information, and of which features are mostly relevant, enabling model-level understanding and debugging. GNANs have been further extended to temporal, heterogeneous data (Bechler-Speicher et al., 2025), to incorporate parameter-efficient transformations (Siddartha Reddy et al., 2025), and to Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLMs (Sade et al., 2026).

Despite the effectiveness of GNANs, in this work we identify the following three limitations that can hinder both their downstream performance and their interpretability:
i) the node-wise importance scores extracted by GNAN for node ii do not represent its own contribution, but are a blurred aggregation of the importances of every node; ii) GNAN relies exclusively on shortest-path distances to encode graph structure, potentially missing other informative topological properties.
iii) GNAN multiplies the univariate feature function with the shortest-path distance reweighting, resulting in a less interpretable mixture of feature, distance, and interaction effects.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce the Attribute-Motif Interaction Graph Additive model (𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}).
𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} relies on motifs automatically discovered from the training set, with each node contributing based on its features and on which motifs it appears in.
The model linearly combines three additive channels – feature, structural, and feature–structure interaction – each centered under a graph-balanced reference distribution that assigns equal mass to each training graph, ensuring the three channels form a unique canonical decomposition.
Summarizing, our main contributions are:

•

We identify three limitations of current graph additive models: node-wise importance scores do not isolate node-local contributions, shortest-path distances miss richer topology, and multiplicative feature–distance coupling obscures the separate feature, distance, and interaction effects.

•

We introduce 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA}, an interpretable-by-design GNN that replaces distance-based aggregation with automatically mined motifs, enabling the model to capture richer structural patterns while providing disentangled feature- and motif-based contributions.

•

We develop a graph-balanced centering scheme that makes the additive decomposition well-defined and unique, allowing predictions to be decomposed into separate attribute, structural, and attribute–structure interaction contributions.

Across ten graph classification and regression benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} outperforms GNAN on eight datasets and G-NAMRFF on nine.
Furthermore, in a controlled experiment, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} successfully recovers the known task composition from label supervision alone, and achieves an explanation accuracy of 0.990.99 and 1.001.00 of AUCROC score on two synthetic datasets with known ground-truth explanations.
Although black-box GNNs remain stronger on most real-world benchmarks, 𝖠𝖬𝖨𝖦𝖠\mathsf{AMIGA} narrows the gap while providing an exact, interpretable decomposition of every prediction.
